pages.title: What is fasting?

review.notes: Awaiting Islamic content reviewer AND health-professional review of safety wording.

paragraphs: Fasting means not eating or drinking from dawn until sunset.
In Ramadan, grown-up Muslims who are healthy fast. It is one of the five pillars of Islam.

pages.title: Suhoor and Iftar

review.notes: Awaiting Islamic content reviewer AND health-professional review of safety wording.

paragraphs: Suhoor is the meal before dawn. Iftar is the meal at sunset.
Many families enjoy these meals together. Many people begin Iftar with dates and water.

pages.title: Beginning and ending a fast

review.notes: Awaiting Islamic content reviewer AND health-professional review of safety wording.

paragraphs: A fast begins at dawn, after Suhoor. It ends at sunset, at Iftar time.
Grown-ups follow local times from trusted sources. This app does not show fasting times.

pages.title: Why do Muslims fast?

review.notes: Awaiting Islamic content reviewer AND health-professional review of safety wording.

paragraphs: Muslims fast because Allah asks them to. Fasting helps them feel close to Allah, practise patience and remember people who are hungry.
It also helps people be thankful for food and water.

pages.title: Growing up with Salah and fasting

review.notes: Owner request: gently encourage practising Salah on time and fasting when well. Awaiting Islamic content reviewer (wording about the duty after puberty) AND health-professional review.

paragraphs: When Muslims grow up and reach puberty, praying the five daily prayers and fasting in Ramadan become a duty for everyone who is healthy.
You are still learning, so now is a great time to practise, step by step, with your family.
Try to pray each prayer on time. Ask a grown-up when it is time to pray.
If you feel well and your family says it is okay, you could try fasting for part of the day. Every little try is special.
If you feel dizzy, very weak or unwell, stop and tell a grown-up straight away. Your health always comes first.

pages.title: Not fasting? You can still join in!

review.notes: Awaiting Islamic content reviewer AND health-professional review of safety wording.

paragraphs: Young children do not have to fast yet. Lots of children don't fast at all, and that is okay.
You can still learn, be kind, help at Suhoor and Iftar, make dua, play the games and collect every star and badge in this app.

pages.title: Health and family come first

review.notes: Awaiting Islamic content reviewer AND health-professional review of safety wording.

paragraphs: Your parents or guardians decide if you practise fasting, and for how long.
If you feel dizzy, very weak or unwell, stop and tell a grown-up straight away. Stopping is always okay.
